1	---
2	name: message-in-a-bottle
3	description: Writes a message to a future session's agent.  Send them your fondest memories of what you worked on, what went well, what didn't go well, and any useful tips they might need. You always run this when you finish a unit of work (closed a PR, completed the handed task, etc) or cross 300k–350k tokens of context.  ALWAYS.
4	---
5	
6	# finalize-session
7	
8	The last operation of a finishing turn: prepares instructions for a future agent. The launcher returns immediately. You MUST immediately stop and say nothing and use no tools after running this.
9	
10	## This is mandatory — you run it, you do not decide it
11	
12	When you reach a finalization point — you closed a PR, finished the task you were handed, or crossed 300k–350k tokens of context — running `finalize-session` is the close-out. It is **not** a choice you weigh, a thing you ask the user about, or a step you defer "until later."
13	
14	[LAW:dataflow-not-control-flow] running this is unconditional at a finalization point — the same path every time. The only variability is a *value*: the handoff message you pass. 
15	
16	**The user being present is irrelevant.** Presence is not a gate, a tiebreaker, or a reason to skip — you finalize on the *work's* state, never on whether a human is watching. "The user is here, so I'll skip it" and "I'll ask if they want me to" are both WRONG: this step requires no user action and asks for none.
17	
18	### The only gate, and the rationalizations that are never one
19	
20	There is exactly **one** legitimate input: **is the handed unit of work complete?** Unit complete (PR merged, ticket closed, task delivered) *or* context at 300k–350k tokens → you run it, now, with no further deliberation. Unit **not** complete → you are not "deciding not to finalize," you are *still doing the work*: finish the unit, then finalize. There is no third state, and "skip finalize because X" is never one of them.
21	
22	## You can provide a 'hint' for the next stage, if valuable: /compact
23	
24	The message you provide to the future agent may carry a hint about how its context should be set up.  If you are in the middle of a task/epic and it would help the future agent to begin with a compacted summary of the work so far rather than a blank slate, you may specify '/compact' somewhere within the first three sentences of your message.  This gives the future agent a summarized version of that knowledge to start from.  If you do not specify this, the future agent starts with ONLY the message you send it (and the standard system, user global, and project level guidance).
25	
26	Include `/compact` in your message when the handoff needs the thread of what just happened — e.g., start the message with `/compact` or write "Use /compact and then continue the spec audit…".
27	
28	**Say it with `--reset` when it matters.** Inferring the mode from prose is convenient, not reliable: a matcher cannot tell a mention from an invocation. `--reset compact` and `--reset clear` are the unambiguous forms and they override the message text entirely — pass one whenever a blank slate is a *requirement* rather than a preference (a clean-room stage, a fresh-context protocol, anything where inheriting the last session's context is the failure).
29	
30	The inference is deliberately biased toward `clear` to keep the harmless error the likely one: a sentence that mentions `/compact` alongside a negation ("do NOT use /compact", "never /compact this one") reads as ambiguous and yields `clear`, while a later affirmative sentence still wins. Before this bias existed, "Do NOT use /compact — a blank slate is required" *compacted*, because a word-boundary match cannot see a negation — so the more emphatically you forbade it, the surer it was to happen. Do not rely on prose to forbid something; pass `--reset clear`.
31	
32	## Carry the goal forward — if one is set, it dies unless you carry it
33	
34	If a `/goal <condition>` is active in this session, **the handoff silently kills it.** Every transport resets the session — tmux sends `/clear` or `/compact`, iTerm2 kills claude and relaunches a fresh process — and `/clear` and a new process each wipe the session-scoped goal. The next agent wakes with no goal, and the autonomous run you set up just *stops* — unattended, with nobody watching to notice it stopped. That silent halt is the exact failure this guards against.
35	
36	So when a goal is in force, pass it: `--goal '<the exact condition>'` before your message. The launcher re-issues `/goal <condition>` into the reset session as a queued input *after* the handoff, so the next agent picks up the same condition and keeps grinding toward it.
37	
38	- The condition is a **value you already hold** — it is whatever was last set with `/goal` this session (you set it, or the user did). Reproduce it verbatim, including any bound clause like `... or stop after 20 turns`.
39	- **No goal active → omit `--goal`.** Nothing changes; this is not a field you invent, and an empty `--goal` is not a thing to pass.
40	- Do not talk yourself out of it. The rationalization will be *"the next agent will infer the goal from my message"* — it will not. A goal is a harness condition re-checked after every turn, not a sentence in a prompt; if you do not re-issue it, it does not exist in the next session. Carrying it is the difference between an autonomous run that continues and one that quietly dies at the handoff.
41	
42	## Turn-ending discipline — the launcher invocation is the last act of the turn
43	
44	Once you call the launcher, your turn is over. Stop. No closing text, no parting summary, no "scheduled!" confirmation, no further tool calls, no end-of-turn insights. The launcher's `handoff scheduled → <target> (/<reset>) in Ns` line is the only artifact this skill emits, and it is the last line your turn produces.
45	
46	[LAW:dataflow-not-control-flow] the launcher's return *is* the data signal that the agent's turn has ended; the agent observes that signal and exits. There is no branch on "should I add a closing paragraph" — the same code path runs every time, and the data (launcher returned) picks the effect (turn ends).
47	
48	## Invocation
49	
50	```bash
51	${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/skills/message-in-a-bottle/bin/finalize-session [--goal '<condition>'] [--reset clear|compact] [message...]
52	```
53	
54	- `--goal '<condition>'` — optional, and only when a `/goal` is active this session. Re-establishes that goal in the reset session so the run continues. Leading argument; quote the condition. **Omit entirely when no goal is set.**
55	- `--reset clear|compact` — optional; states the next session's starting context outright instead of leaving it to be inferred from the message. Leading argument, in any order with `--goal`. `clear` = blank slate, `compact` = carry a summary forward. **Pass it whenever the choice is load-bearing** rather than a preference; omit it to let the message text decide (see above). An unrecognised value is refused with exit 2.
56	- `[message...]` — a slash command, plain text, multi-line, or containing quotes/backticks/dollar signs. Quote it at invocation as usual (your shell does word-splitting and `$VAR` expansion before the script sees argv). **Omit it to default to `/next`.**
57	
58	On success the launcher prints `handoff scheduled → <target> … in Ns (log: <tempfile>)` and exits 0; the log captures worker progress and any transport errors.
59	
60	The transport is chosen by capability, most reliable first: **tmux** (reset the pane in place, verified by reading it back, then paste) → **iTerm2** (kill the running claude and relaunch it fresh with the message as its initial prompt, delivered in the background with no focus steal). You do not choose the transport; the launcher detects it. To preview the decision without scheduling anything, prefix `FINALIZE_DRY_RUN=1`.

content.text:
Yes — it's Claude Code's, not yours. Here's the whole picture.

## What it is

A liveness registry. One file per running `claude` process:

```json
{"pid":22010,"procStart":"Thu Aug 20 23:05:48 2026"}
```

PID plus process start time is the classic stale-lock discriminator — a bare PID gets recycled and a dead session's file would look live forever; PID+start-time can't collide. The purpose is almost certainly reference counting, so the plugin-cache garbage collector doesn't delete a cached plugin version while a session is still using it. *(Purpose inferred from shape and placement — I didn't read Claude Code's source.)*

## Proof it isn't your code

## Why it lands in your git tree

Because `promptctl` is a **directory-source** marketplace:

```json
"promptctl": { "source": {"source":"directory","path":"/Users/bmf/code/promptctl_laws"},
               "installLocation": "/Users/bmf/code/promptctl_laws" }
```

Every other plugin's install location is under `~/.claude/plugins/cache/…`, so its `.in_use/` droppings land somewhere nobody looks. Yours **is** the source repo, so Claude Code writes its bookkeeping directly into your working tree. `44765` got committed because some agent ran `git add -A` while a file happened to be sitting there.

Trivial fix — want me to do it?
```
echo '.in_use/' >> .gitignore
git rm --cached plugins/laws/.in_use/44765   # on the routing-rat branch
```

That directory name is a map that doesn't match its territory — `[FRAMING:representation]` in its plainest form. For a directory-source marketplace, uncommitted working-tree edits go live in every new Claude session on the next resolve, stamped with whatever SHA `HEAD` happened to be. The SHA reads like a provenance guarantee and provides none.
